blocks.p: This done, but not yet thinking himself secure enough, he next set about remodeling the town, setting up one and putting down another as he pleased. So my Lord Mayor, whose name was my Lord Understanding, and Mr. Recorder, whose name was Mr. Conscience, he put out of place and power.

As for my Lord Mayor: though he was an understanding man, and one who had gone along with the rest of the town of Mansoul in letting the giant in, Diabolus still did not think it fit to let him keep his former luster and glory, because he was a seeing man. So he darkened him, not only by taking away his office and power, but by building a high, strong tower right between the sun’s rays and the windows of my lord’s palace. By this means his house, and his whole dwelling, was made as dark as darkness itself; and so, cut off from the light, he became like a man born blind. My lord was confined to this house of his as to a prison, and he was not allowed, even on his word of honor, to go beyond his own bounds. And now, even if he had had a heart to help Mansoul, what could he do for her? So for as long as Mansoul was under the power and government of Diabolus (and she was under him as long as she obeyed him, which was until she was rescued out of his hand by war), my Lord Mayor was more of a hindrance than a help to the famous town of Mansoul.

As for Mr. Recorder: before the town was taken, he was a man well read in the laws of his King, and also a man of courage and faithfulness, ready to speak the truth on every occasion; and he had a tongue as boldly hung as his head was full of judgment. Now Diabolus could not stand this man, because although the Recorder had consented to his coming into the town, the giant could not, with all the tricks, trials, schemes, and devices he could use, make him wholly his own. True, he had fallen far from his former King, and he was much pleased with many of the giant’s laws and services; but all this would not do, since he was not wholly the giant’s. Now and then he would think of Shaddai, and feel the dread of his law upon him, and then he would speak against Diabolus with a voice as loud as a lion’s roar. Yes, and at certain times, when his fits were on him (for you must know that he sometimes had terrible fits), he would make the whole town of Mansoul shake with his voice. And so the present king of Mansoul could not stand him.

So Diabolus feared the Recorder more than anyone left alive in the town of Mansoul, because, as I said, his words shook the whole town; they were like rolling thunder, and like thunderclaps too. Since the giant could not make him wholly his own, then, what does he do but put all his study into corrupting the old gentleman, and by corruption dulling his mind and hardening his heart further in the ways of vanity. And as he attempted, so he succeeded. Little by little he drew the man so far into sin and wickedness that at last he was not only corrupted, and so defiled, but almost (at last, I say) past all sense of sin. And this was as far as Diabolus could go. So he thought of another project, and that was to persuade the men of the town that Mr. Recorder was mad, and therefore not to be listened to. For this he pointed to his fits. “If he is in his right mind,” he said, “why doesn’t he act like this all the time? But just as all madmen have their fits, and their raving talk in them, so does this old and doting gentleman.”

So by one means or another he quickly got Mansoul to slight, neglect, and despise whatever Mr. Recorder could say. For besides what you have already heard, Diabolus had a way of making the old gentleman, when he was in a merry mood, take back and deny what he had declared in his fits. And indeed, this was the surest way to make him ridiculous, so that no one would pay attention to him. Also, he never spoke freely for King Shaddai now, but only under force and constraint. Besides, at one time he would be hot against something about which at another time he would say nothing, so uneven was he now in his doings. Sometimes he would be as if fast asleep, and at other times as if dead, even when the whole town of Mansoul was in full career after vanity, dancing to the giant’s pipe.

So sometimes, when Mansoul had been frightened by the thundering voice of the man who had been their Recorder, and they told Diabolus about it, he would answer that what the old gentleman said came from no love for him and no pity for them, but from a foolish fondness for chattering; and so he would hush them, calm them, and make everything quiet again. And so as to leave no argument unused that might make them feel secure, he said, and said it often, “O Mansoul, consider that for all the old gentleman’s rage, and the rattle of his lofty, thundering words, you hear nothing from Shaddai himself.” Yet, liar and deceiver that he was, every outcry of Mr. Recorder against the sin of Mansoul was the voice of God in him, speaking to them. But Diabolus goes on and says, “You see that Shaddai cares nothing for the loss or the rebellion of the town of Mansoul, and will not trouble himself to call his town to account for giving themselves to me. He knows that though you were his, you are now lawfully mine; so he has left us to each other, and washed his hands of us.

“Moreover, O Mansoul,” he said, “consider how I have served you, to the utmost of my power, and with the best that I have, or could get, or could obtain for you in all the world. Besides, I dare say that the laws and customs you are now under, by which you do homage to me, give you more comfort and contentment than the paradise you had at first. Your liberty, too, as you yourselves know very well, has been greatly widened and enlarged by me, whereas I found you a penned-up people. I have laid no restraint on you. You have no law, statute, or judgment of mine to frighten you. I call none of you to account for what you do, except the madman (you know whom I mean). I have granted you to live, each man like a prince in his own domain, with as little control from me as I myself have from you.”

So Diabolus would quiet the town whenever their old Recorder troubled them; yes, and with cursed speeches like these he would set the whole town in a rage and fury against the old gentleman. At times the rascal crew were even for destroying him. They often wished, in my hearing, that he lived a thousand miles away from them. His company, his words, even the sight of him, terrified and afflicted them sorely, especially when they remembered how in the old days he used to threaten and condemn them (corrupted as he now was).

But all their wishes were in vain; for I do not know how, unless by the power and wisdom of Shaddai, he was preserved alive among them. Besides, his house was as strong as a castle, and stood close to a stronghold of the town. Moreover, if at any time any of the crew or rabble tried to do away with him, he could pull up the sluices and let in such floods as would drown everything around him.

But to leave Mr. Recorder and come to my Lord Willbewill, another of the gentry of the famous town of Mansoul. This Willbewill was as high-born as any man in Mansoul, and as much a freeholder as many of them, if not more; besides, if I remember my tale correctly, he had some privileges peculiar to himself. Along with these, he was a man of great strength, resolution, and courage, and once he set himself to a thing, no one could turn him from it. But I say, whether he was proud of his estate, his privileges, his strength, or what (but it was surely through pride of something), he now scorns to be a slave in Mansoul, and so resolves to hold office under Diabolus, so that he might (such a man as he was) be a petty ruler and governor in Mansoul. And, headstrong man that he was, he began early: for when Diabolus made his speech at Ear-gate, this man was one of the first to agree with his words and to accept his counsel as wholesome, and was for opening the gate and letting him into the town. So Diabolus had a fondness for him, and planned a place for him. And seeing the man’s valor and boldness, he wanted him as one of his great ones, to act and manage in matters of the highest concern.

So he sent for him and opened the secret matter that lay in his heart; but little persuasion was needed. For as he had been willing at first for Diabolus to be let into the town, so now he was just as willing to serve him there. So when the tyrant saw that my lord’s mind was bending his way, he at once made him captain of the castle, governor of the wall, and keeper of the gates of Mansoul. Indeed, there was a clause in his commission that nothing should be done in all the town of Mansoul without him. So now, next to Diabolus himself, who was there but my Lord Willbewill in all the town of Mansoul? Nothing could be done anywhere in the town except at his will and pleasure. He also had one Mr. Mind for his clerk, a man who spoke in every way like his master; for he and his lord were one in principle, and not far apart in practice. And now Mansoul was brought under in earnest, and made to fulfill the cravings of the will and of the mind.

But I cannot get out of my thoughts what a desperate man this Willbewill was once power was put into his hands. First, he flatly denied that he owed any duty or service to his former prince and rightful lord. That done, he next took an oath and swore loyalty to his great master Diabolus. And then, once he was established and settled in his positions, offices, advancements, and promotions, oh, you cannot imagine, unless you had seen it, the strange work this workman did in the town of Mansoul.

First, he hated Mr. Recorder to the death. He could not bear to see him, or to hear the words of his mouth; he would shut his eyes when he saw him and stop his ears when he heard him speak. He also could not bear that so much as a fragment of the law of Shaddai should be seen anywhere in the town. For example, his clerk, Mr. Mind, had some old, ragged, torn parchments of the law of Shaddai in his house; but when Willbewill saw them, he threw them behind his back. True, Mr. Recorder had some of the laws in his study, but my lord could by no means get at them. He also thought, and said, that the windows of my old Lord Mayor’s house were always too light for the good of the town of Mansoul. He could not bear even the light of a candle. Nothing at all pleased Willbewill now but what pleased Diabolus his lord.

There was no one like him for trumpeting about the streets the fine nature, the wise conduct, and the great glory of King Diabolus. He would range and roam through all the streets of Mansoul to cry up his illustrious lord, and would make himself an outcast among the base and rascally crew to cry up his valiant prince. And I say, whenever and wherever he found these hangers-on, he would make himself one of them. In every evil course he would act unbidden, and do mischief without command.

The Lord Willbewill also had a deputy under him named Mr. Affection, another man badly corrupted in his principles, and living to match. He was wholly given to the flesh, and so they called him Vile-Affection. Now he and one Carnal-Lust, the daughter of Mr. Mind (like to like), fell in love, made a match, and were married; and as I understand it, they had several children: Impudent, Blackmouth, and Hate-Reproof. These three were black-hearted boys. Besides these they had three daughters, Scorn-Truth and Slight-God, and the youngest was named Revenge. These all married in the town, and they too had many bad brats, too many to list here. But I will pass this by.

When the giant had garrisoned himself in the town of Mansoul in this way, and had put down and set up whomever he thought good, he set himself to defacing. Now there was in the marketplace of Mansoul, and also on the gates of the castle, an image of the blessed King Shaddai. This image was so exactly engraved (and it was engraved in gold) that it resembled Shaddai himself more than anything else then in the world. This he basely commanded to be defaced, and it was as basely done by the hand of Mr. No-Truth. And when it had been defaced, he gave orders that the same Mr. No-Truth should set up in its place the horrid and fearsome image of Diabolus, to the great contempt of the former King and the debasing of his town of Mansoul.

Moreover, Diabolus made havoc of whatever remained of the laws and statutes of Shaddai that could be found in the town of Mansoul: such as contained the teachings of morality, along with all civil and natural instruction. He also set out to stamp out the strict duties people owed one another in their relations. In short, there was nothing left of good in Mansoul that he and Willbewill did not seek to destroy; for their design was to turn Mansoul into a brute, and make it like the sensual sow, by the hand of Mr. No-Truth.

When he had destroyed what law and good order he could, then, to carry his design further (namely, to turn Mansoul away from Shaddai her King), he commanded his own empty edicts, statutes, and commandments to be set up, and they set them up, in every place where people met and gathered in Mansoul: such as gave free rein to “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life,” which are not of Shaddai but of the world [1 John 2:16]. He encouraged, approved, and promoted lewdness and every kind of ungodliness there. Indeed, Diabolus did much more to encourage wickedness in the town of Mansoul: he promised them peace, contentment, joy, and bliss in doing his commands, and that they would never be called to account for not doing the contrary. And let this serve to give a taste to those who love to hear of things done far off in other countries, beyond their own knowledge.
Now Mansoul being wholly at his beck and call, and brought wholly under his bow, nothing was heard or seen there but what tended to set him up.

But now, having disabled the Lord Mayor and Mr. Recorder from holding office in Mansoul, and seeing that the town, before he came to it, was the most ancient corporation in the world, he feared that if he did not keep up its greatness, they might at some time object that he had done them an injury. So, I say (so that they might see he did not intend to lessen their grandeur, or take from them any of their advantages), he chose a Lord Mayor and a Recorder for them himself, men who contented them to the heart, and who also pleased him wonderfully well.

The name of the Mayor of Diabolus’s making was the Lord Lustings, a man ruled by his appetites, who had neither eyes nor ears. All that he did, whether as a man or as an officer, he did by mere nature, as a beast does. And what made him more ignoble still (though not to Mansoul, but to those who looked on and grieved over its ruin) was that he could never favor good, but only evil.

The Recorder was a man named Forget-Good, and a very sorry fellow he was. He could remember nothing but mischief, and doing it with delight. He was by nature inclined to do harmful things, harmful even to the town of Mansoul and everyone who lived there. So these two, by their power and practice, their example, and their smiles on evil, did much to school the common people in harmful ways and settle them there. For who does not see that when those in high places are vile and corrupt themselves, they corrupt the whole region and country where they are?

Besides these, Diabolus made several burgesses and aldermen in Mansoul, from among whom the town, when it needed, might choose its officers, governors, and magistrates. These are the names of the chief of them: Mr. Incredulity (that is, unbelief), Mr. Haughty, Mr. Swearing, Mr. Whoring, Mr. Hard-Heart, Mr. Pitiless, Mr. Fury, Mr. No-Truth, Mr. Stand-to-Lies, Mr. False-Peace, Mr. Drunkenness, Mr. Cheating, and Mr. Atheism, thirteen in all. Mr. Incredulity is the eldest, and Mr. Atheism the youngest of the company.

Common councilmen were elected too, with bailiffs, sergeants, constables, and others; but all were like those already named, being their fathers, brothers, cousins, or nephews, and for brevity’s sake I leave out their names.

When the giant had gone this far in his work, he next set about building some strongholds in the town, and he built three that seemed impregnable. The first he called the Hold of Defiance, because it was made to command the whole town and keep it from the knowledge of its ancient King. The second he called Midnight Hold, because it was built on purpose to keep Mansoul from the true knowledge of itself. The third was called Sweet-Sin Hold, because by it he fortified Mansoul against every desire for good. The first of these strongholds stood close by Eye-gate, so that, as far as possible, the light might be darkened there. The second was built hard by the old castle, so that the castle might be made blinder still, if that were possible. And the third stood in the marketplace.

Over the first of these Diabolus made one Spite-God governor, a most blasphemous wretch. He came with the whole rabble that came against Mansoul at first, and was one of them himself. The one made governor of Midnight Hold was one Love-no-Light; he too was one of those who came against the town at first. And the one made governor of the stronghold called Sweet-Sin Hold was a man named Love-Flesh. He too was a very lewd fellow, but not from the country where the others are kept in chains. This fellow could find more sweetness in sucking on a lust than in all the paradise of God.

And now Diabolus thought himself safe. He had taken Mansoul; he had garrisoned himself in it; he had put down the old officers and set up new ones; he had defaced the image of Shaddai and set up his own; he had spoiled the old law books and promoted his own empty lies; he had made himself new magistrates and set up new aldermen; he had built himself new strongholds and manned them for himself. And all this he did to make himself secure, in case the good Shaddai, or his Son, should come to make an incursion against him.
